title: I need some game design help with this project
author: Square-Yam-3772
selftext:
so I have this concept of a game as presented by this video (I haven't built a playable demo yet, this is just a generated video)

basically it is a monster battle + bullet hell + roguelike + 3-choose-1 upgrade mechanics 

...and I am stuck because I don't know what features/mechanics/idea can make this fun

can bullet hell fans from this sub help me brainstorm the gamedesign with me on this thread?

I can't go to other subs because they will probably get into some anti rants  

here is what I got:

* players can unlock new monsters from runs
* monsters should be unique (their own upgrade lists?)
* maybe some timer that activates the 3-choose-1 upgrades (since there are no mobs to kill for exp)
* ???

I got nothing else. Please help. thanks

replies.author: Segaiai
replies.body:
I ran a game development group for a good while almost decades ago. This mindset was extremely common back then too. The only difference is that they didn't have a program that would make whatever they told it to make, so they didn't get a playable anything. They just walked around telling people about their brilliant idea that wasn't even a game concept. 

They simply strung together some impressive sounding features and expected other people to be impressed. The lack of ability forced some of them to learn coding skills the hard way, which forced them into just making squares move around on a screen, and in doing that, they learned game design because that's the only part they could "play" with at that skill level. The only ones who didn't learn were those who never started skill building, and that includes the people rich enough to pay others to make their brilliant string of impressive sounding features.

Anyway, I think this generation isn't cooked. This is the normal beginner mindset. Beginners have to fail to learn stuff like this, and in failing, this person is going to learn what game design ACTUALLY is by prototyping without any art after a bit of roasting online. There's a new layer of confusion when they get people to say wow on their visuals, and if AI is doing too much coding, they won't know how to do things like tweak movement to get great gamefeel, but again, they'll just encounter some roasting and if they care enough about their project, they'll dig in and actually learn skills. Those barriers do make it harder to know the path to building skill though, so that's unfortunate. I just don't think they're worse off than previous generations as a starting point.

replies.author: fyndor
replies.body: You start with the fun.  You don't start with art and ask "how do I make this art fun".  You are starting from the wrong direction.  You should be starting with greyboxing. replies.author: CuriousGio
replies.body:
Make it fun. Period. Don't get bogged down in mythology, technology, cool graphics, etc. 

TBH: you need to decide what your goal is, to make money, to make a good game but it's modeled after another successful game, or, to create a game that's shaped by fun no matter how strange and quirky it gets.

If you have good taste, and you create a game that you personally love and a game you would be excited about if somebody else designed it —meaning, IF, in a parallel world, the moment you see a video of this game you're making, you're so excited, you start counting the days to its release date. 

My convoluted point is, if choose to pursue a game that excites you, & you execute on the concept, your chance at succes is much higher.

It sounds like you're disconnected from your instincts. You're looking outward for validation when only you can decide what your game should be. Nobody else knows what type of mechanics you love. 

It's essential that you figure out what's driving you to want to make this game. I've read other comments giving you similar advice so I'm just another voice among many.

I say this because I understand the feeling. I've been there. You want nothing else but to create something cool, and you have a high level concept that you're excited about, but you feel stuck before you've even begun the journey. It's frustrating.

Tell me if I'm wrong.

I think I understand where you're at.

What's unique about your concept? Is there anything fresh about your idea? Ideas are easy. Not all ideas translate into a good game. If you have to work hard to see the game, it's either not the great idea that you think it is, OR, you're not good at designing games.

It sounds like you've designed games before, from what I read. If that's true, why are you feeling stuck with this concept? What's different about this idea?

My 2.5 cents

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
Your concept video has no movement. A bullet hell game is all about dodging bullets and attacks whilst attacking the enemies simultaneously. They typically have fast paced combat. I would suggest going to play some and studying the mechanics of the combat.

In terms of upgrades, look at roguelikes like Risk of Rain, Brotato, Vampire Survivors, etc. The whole premise of those games is to choose upgrades wisely so that your upgrades and weapons synergise into powerful builds. You need enough variety that it isn't boring, but a small enough set of upgrades that it's not overwhelming and new players can quickly see synergies. It's a hard thing to balance and generally takes a lot of play testing to get right.

comments.author: Shalcker
comments.body:
You could ask AI for ideas, it isn't that complicated and you got to try different things and build your own intuition on what works and what doesn't either way, you aren't going straight to "final form" without trial and error. What exactly you rejected from AI suggestions you tried would be also helpful.

But if I were to go with this idea, i'd go with:  
\- make those "bullet hell" bullets and effects counter each other - so large bullet absorb small bullets, maybe slow down, and then disappears if hit enough times.  
\- monsters could have (upgradeable) shields from certain angles that deflect and absorb hits of certain types (probably color and shape coded)  
\- monsters themselves can have limited (upgradeable) dodging potential to avoid individual hits or get them on shields specifically; if they are controlled you could upgrade movement speed/turn speed/dash length  
\- obviously they have "skills" that emit certain kinds of bullets with certain trajectory - those can have increased damage, increased duration, increased fire rate, and lowered cooldown  
\- perhaps interactions between different kinds of bullets creating different effects (shrapnel, split bullets, explosions, type switching, lingering ground/air effects like poison clouds or fire patches)

From technical side you need very lightweight system for bullets, and in general be careful with "lots of things on the screen" - easy to get trapped in a system that is too slow due to each individual object being too complex, even with modern processing power.
